frontier.hypothesis: Ten of the fifteen remaining points are register NAMES, not instructions: the hoisted 0x91A2B3C5 constant takes $t2 and pushes the mfhi temp to $t3. If that hoisted pseudo can be steered to a different hard register, the floor drops to about 5 without touching the loop.c:1631 decision at all - and nobody has looked at this axis yet, because s1-s3 treated the whole residual as one indivisible LICM problem.
frontier.mechanism: After the hoist, the constant pseudo is a global allocno live across the whole of loop 2 and is coloured before the loop's short-lived mfhi temp; global.c's allocno priority ordering and the local-alloc suggestion pass decide which of $t1/$t2/$t3 each gets. The target's allocation has $t1 = 0x88888889 and $t2 = the mfhi temp, so only ONE seat has to move.

Do NOT start from the LICM question - this is a pure seat problem and it is worth 10 of the 15 points.

frontier.hypothesis: The 15-point body's two non-ordinary constructs - the split accumulators (flags/flags0/flags1/flags2) and the `i = 0;` hoist - still need an admissibility ruling before any submission, and respelling them to dodge that is the wrong move. Carried unchanged from s3.
frontier.mechanism: Neither construct is dead and neither is a coercion: every split local is written once and holds a value that IS stored to p[8] and read by the next arm, and `i = 0;` is the loop's real initialisation. But flags0 and flags1 are each read TWICE (the store and the next arm), so this is not the once-written/once-read named-intermediate shape in .claude/rules/narrow-byte-args-packed-call.md, and the only reason not to reuse one `v` is codegen.
